title: Becquerel vs Curie: Radioactivity Units and Sample Sizes
description: 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq = 37 GBq. Medical isotopes in MBq to GBq; environmental samples in Bq; regulatory limits mix both.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Bq is one decay per second. Ci is 3.7 × 10¹⁰ of them. Twelve orders of magnitude, one unit conversion.
body: Activity measures the rate of nuclear decays. The SI unit (becquerel) is trivially small — one decay per second — so real sources are always quoted in prefixed forms (kBq, MBq, GBq) or in the legacy curie.

> 1 Bq = 1 decay per second
> 1 Ci = 3.7 × 10¹⁰ Bq = 37 GBq (defined by original radium standard)
> 1 mCi = 37 MBq; 1 µCi = 37 kBq

Bq: environmental measurements, food safety limits, radon in air. kBq/MBq: laboratory tracers. GBq: nuclear medicine doses, industrial radiography sources. Ci: US regulatory language, older US medical literature. TBq/kCi: reactor inventories.
Banana ⁴⁰K activity: ~15 Bq. Radon action level (EPA): 148 Bq/m³ = 4 pCi/L. Bone scan dose: 800 MBq ⁹⁹ᵐTc. Cs-137 sealed source (calibration): 10–100 MBq.

Prescription: 20 mCi ⁹⁹ᵐTc-MDP. Equivalent 740 MBq. The dose calibrator reads in mCi; the modern regulatory paperwork wants MBq. Miss the 37× factor and you either dispense 27 mCi (30× overdose in old units — but actually right in MBq) or underdose by the same factor. Real errors traced to this exact conversion have reached patients.
1 Ci = 37 GBq. Modern practice is Bq; US clinical still runs on mCi/µCi.

faqs.q: Is activity the same as dose?
faqs.a: No — activity is decays per second; dose is energy per kg received by tissue. Both matter separately.
Historically defined as the activity of 1 g of radium-226. Later redefined as an exact number but retained the same value.
